visible.summary:
Turkmenistan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 135 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 2 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Absence of documentation is itself evidence of severity: data collection is impossible because it is unsafe.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 Criminal Code not only kept the 'sodomy' provisions but increased both the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the country with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them — the current penal-risk read.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Turkmenistan: lists among significant human-rights issues the existence of laws criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity — official assessment of law plus enforcement climate.

EHPV mid-term UPR stakeholder submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the Criminal Code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

ECOM legislative analysis, 'Legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan' (Tallinn, 2019, 11pp, with Turkmen.news): maps the legal landscape and barriers for LGBT people and PLHIV — deliberately compiled so NGOs, community activists and government can use it when planning advocacy; the standing legal-baseline reference for the country.

Columbia Law School (May 1, 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum (DHS) for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

visible.summary:
Syria is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.
visible.tangentialFactors: Articles 520/517 criminalise “sexual acts against nature” — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General conflict risk affects all; the 2025 trans-women violence waves are trans-specific.

sources.claim: GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025 on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.
thin: no usable finding

Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.

visible.summary:
Libya is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises “illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” (up to 5 years), and Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and transition through these provisions — compounded by recent religious rulings declaring the very term “gender” haram, making anyone using it in media or institutions susceptible to prosecution. Militias control territory and operate detention sites where torture is systematic; there is no functioning central judiciary, no LGR, and no protection of any kind.

For a visitor: detention by any of several militia authorities is the modal bad outcome, with no consular reach in much of the country.
visible.tangentialFactors: “Illicit sexual intercourse” and “indecent acts” provisions (up to 5 years) capture same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity alike.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Militia fragmentation means enforcement varies by territory; the trans-specific mechanism is documented de-facto criminalisation.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review: Libya has de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process (social, medical, surgical), enforced through 'indecent acts' and 'illicit intercourse' provisions; recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not legal for men or women; 'indecent acts' provisions carry up to 5 years' imprisonment; no legal protections against SOGI discrimination; same-sex relationships not legally recognised; legal gender recognition unavailable (official identity documents cannot be changed); LGBTI organisations cannot register.

The Guardian, Brian Whitaker guide (21 Jun 2016): Libya is among regional states where homosexuality carries imprisonment as the penalty (specific terms vary by country); where no specific law exists, other laws are used — the guide assesses the catastrophic effect of these regimes on gay people's lives.

HRW (8 Jun 2015): documents Islamic State's killing of men accused of homosexuality in territory it controlled, including Derna, Libya — a young man there was targeted by local Islamists for effeminate dress and 'contemporary' clothes (case named from Nov 2014).

D+C (Jun 2015): Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in Derna in April 2015; the piece reports information in Derna flows only through the mosque and concludes the situation for homosexuals in Libya is getting worse as militias control territory.
HuffPost (26 Nov 2012): 12 men accused of being gay faced torture and threatened death at the hands of a Libyan militia — early post-revolutionary vigilante violence against suspected gay men.

visible.summary:
Yemen is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but Cairo 52 emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Houthi-controlled areas impose their own moral-policing regime; the south has its own militia authorities.

For a visitor: no safe authority to appeal to anywhere in the country.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to death under some interpretations; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise) — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: War risk affects all; the documented surge in trans-targeted attacks is trans-specific.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of Yemen: erosion of the rule of law plus humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands (vigilante risk); critically, the penal provisions apply ONLY in government-controlled regions — other areas sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so legal exposure varies by territory.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018, MENA): Yemen is one of 14 covered countries where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited; the report could identify NO activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work (a documented safety gap), and notes 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression.

HRW World Report 2026, Yemen chapter (events of 2025): its Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section states Yemen's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside world's-worst humanitarian crisis (19.5M needing aid) and Houthi/government factional control affecting where law applies.

Amnesty International (Feb 2024): two Huthi-run courts in Yemen sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct — the Dhamar criminal court (23 Jan) sentenced nine to death (seven by stoning, two by crucifixion) with 23 more given 6 months-10 years for 'homosexuality'/'spreading immorality', and an Ibb court (1 Feb) handed further death sentences; Amnesty demanded an immediate halt.

GayLawNet Yemen laws page: consensual same-sex sex is unlawful under Penal Code 1994 Article 264 — homosexuality between men defined as anal penetration; unmarried men punishable with 100 lashes (and up to one year's imprisonment per the statute); the canonical statute citation for Yemen's criminalisation.

IPS (16 Aug 2013) 'No Place for Gays in Yemen': Sana'a social climate — a gay man describes hiding (hood over long hair) as 'still problematic'; conservative society has no place for them while the law sees homosexuality as punishable by death; illustrates discretionary-social enforcement layered on the statutory penalty.

visible.summary:
Bhutan is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression.

Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2021 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the 4x assault likelihood and violence/discrimination reports describe residents' experience.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised in 2021, but there is no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists call the process lengthy and burdensome. Legal gender recognition is unavailable — earlier administrative gender-marker changes are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines. Discrimination and stigma persist, especially in health-care access.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report violence — police dismiss her cases because her identity card reads male ('both parties are men'), families pressure victims to accept it as fate, and help routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. Practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness' (31 Mar 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General's Office and Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first-ever direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians; two consultation workshops convened community members with UN and National Commission for Women and Children representatives.

Erasing 76 Crimes (10 Jun 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted 43-1 to repeal Penal Code Sections 213-214 'unnatural sex' provisions (1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); upper-house ratification still pending at that point. Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (11 Mar 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 Feb 2021 — after the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation (global criminalising-state tally fell 72 to 71). Freshness pass (2026-09-27) confirms this stands with no post-2021 reversal.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow': the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page (from c.2014) produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population; profiles admins and Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira — a first in Bhutanese society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

The Daily Beast (28 Oct 2015): Bhutan's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility — 'growing up gay in Bhutan was a very alienating experience', no shared language for gay or trans identities, lesbianism under-recognised. Karma Dupchen, one of the most public LGBT figures, founded the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page in 2013.

visible.summary:
Namibia demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
visible.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct technically remains criminalised under the common law (unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 legislative backlash signals trajectory.
visible.localsOnly: The earlier document-change court wins are per-case resident litigation; implementation gaps documented by SALC are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Washington Blade op-ed (22 May 2024) by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre: Namibia's Supreme Court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the Immigration Act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell litigant Digashu himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than 'all persons'. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - regional framework document; Namibia's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Namibia' (2017): constitutional analysis - Article 10 omits gender identity/sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the UN Human Rights Committee; section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per the Legal Assistance Centre (2015).

Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.' The article notes the colonial-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence in 1990, and recalls 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation.

Mambaonline (12 December 2018): dozens marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in Namibia. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

Daily Maverick (26 June 2014): a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in the record's political environment.
